clue.text: Brown was his father

parts.note: Brown is the priest-detective Father Brown, so the man who fathered him is the writer who created the character

explanation.surface: A family note: someone's dad was a man named Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' reads as a parent, but Father Brown is a Catholic priest-detective; the 'father' of the character is the author who invented him.
explanation.definitionFit: G. K. Chesterton wrote the Father Brown detective stories, making him the character's literary creator.

clue.text: Roman statesman a turncoat

parts.note: the word is read as an instruction: the letters of coat are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A Roman politician is accused of switching sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turncoat' looks like an accusation of betrayal; split it as 'turn coat' and rearrange C-O-A-T. The 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Cato the Elder and Cato the Younger were both prominent statesmen of the Roman Republic.

clue.text: Lamb (new) in film studio

indicators.note: the bracketed new is placed inside the studio's name

parts.note: Ealing Studios in west London, famous for its postwar comedies

explanation.surface: A new lamb appears in a picture made at a film studio.
explanation.walkthrough: EALING is a London film studio known for the Ealing comedies; put N (new) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An eanling is an archaic word for a young lamb, newly born, used by Shakespeare.

clue.text: Shakespeare's epiphany

parts.note: the play by Shakespeare whose title names the feast of the Epiphany on 6 January

explanation.surface: The playwright has a sudden flash of insight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'epiphany' suggests a revelation, but the Epiphany is the church feast whose eve gives the title of a Shakespeare comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelfth night after Christmas is the feast of Epiphany, and Shakespeare's comedy takes that festive name.

clue.text: They are well versed in Farsi

definitions.text: They are well versed in Farsi

parts.words: They are well versed in Farsi
parts.note: the reference is to a famous set of Persian poems in quatrains, literally verses written in Persian

explanation.surface: Some people are fluent in the Persian language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well versed' means expert, but here it is literal: these are verses, the quatrains of Omar Khayyam that FitzGerald translated.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rubaiyat is Omar Khayyam's collection of Persian quatrains, famous in English through Edward FitzGerald's version.

clue.text: "It shall be what — I say it is" (The Taming of the Shrew)

definitions.text: "It shall be what — I say it is" (The Taming of the Shrew)

parts.words: "It shall be what — I say it is" (The Taming of the Shrew)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the dash marks the missing word in Petruchio's line about the time of day

explanation.surface: A domineering line quoted from Shakespeare's comedy about taming a wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Petruchio insists the hour is whatever he says, to bend Katherina to his will: 'It shall be what o'clock I say it is.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes the phrase for telling the time, so the line names the hour he chooses.

clue.text: Such a man is a paltry thing, said Yeats

definitions.text: Such a man is a paltry thing, said Yeats

parts.words: Such a man is a paltry thing, said Yeats
parts.note: points to the opening of Sailing to Byzantium, where Yeats describes an elderly man as a paltry thing

explanation.surface: Yeats is quoted dismissing a certain kind of man.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats's 'Sailing to Byzantium' says 'An aged man is but a paltry thing, / A tattered coat upon a stick'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in Yeats's line describes an old man, one advanced in years.

clue.text: Style of bookbinding for distinguished publisher of encyclopaedias?

definitions.meaning: a decorative binding style with interlaced gilt strapwork
an American firm that published the Encyclopedia Americana and the Book of Knowledge

explanation.surface: A fine binding suits a great reference publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the pun: the bookbinding style is named after the sixteenth-century French bibliophile, while the publisher is a modern American company sharing his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one surname: a gilt binding style after a French book collector, and a reference-book company named for him.

clue.text: Absurd dramatist, in turn dreamt absurdly

indicators.note: the letters of turn dreamt are arranged in a ridiculous, nonsensical way

explanation.surface: A playwright of the absurd tosses and turns, dreaming nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absurdly' rearranges TURN DREAMT; 'in' is a link. Friedrich Dürrenmatt, the Swiss playwright, is written here without the umlaut.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Dürrenmatt wrote grotesque, darkly comic plays such as The Visit, often linked with the Theatre of the Absurd.

clue.text: She lived for applause 4

parts.note: the fairy in Peter Pan who revives only when the audience claps to show they believe in fairies

explanation.surface: A performer who existed only to hear the audience clap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lived for applause' sounds like an attention-seeker, but in Barrie's Peter Pan the fairy is literally kept alive by the audience's clapping.
explanation.definitionFit: In J. M. Barrie's play the dying fairy is saved when children clap, so applause keeps her alive.

clue.text: Secure Othello

definitions.meaning: to fasten a boat to a quay or buoy
Shakespeare's tragic hero is called the ... of Venice

explanation.surface: Lock up Shakespeare's jealous general.
explanation.definitionFit: Tying up a ship is mooring it, and Othello's title is 'the Moor of Venice', a North African.

clue.text: One of those who, admittedly, was not the very button on Fortune's cap

definitions.text: One of those who, admittedly, was not the very button on Fortune's cap

parts.words: One of those who, admittedly, was not the very button on Fortune's cap
parts.note: Hamlet's schoolfellow who says 'On Fortune's cap we are not the very button'

explanation.surface: Someone concedes he was never at the top of fortune's favour.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet II.ii, Rosencrantz and his companion admit 'On Fortune's cap we are not the very button'; this speaker is the latter.
explanation.definitionFit: Guildenstern, paired with Rosencrantz, speaks the line about not being the very button on Fortune's cap.

clue.text: Willingly page, say

indicators.note: signals the word for page is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: a leaf is a page of a book

explanation.surface: A volunteer page boy goes along gladly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'page' looks like a young servant, but it is a sheet of a book, a LEAF; 'say' turns it into its soundalike LIEF.
explanation.definitionFit: Lief is an archaic adverb meaning gladly, as in 'I would as lief stay'.

clue.text: Like Sherston's memoirs

parts.note: Siegfried Sassoon's trilogy was collected as The Complete Memoirs of George Sherston

explanation.surface: Something resembling a fictional soldier's recollections.
explanation.walkthrough: Sassoon's three Sherston books were gathered as The Complete Memoirs of George Sherston: 'complete' is the word the clue wants a synonym for.
explanation.definitionFit: The collected edition is called complete, and taking in everything is a synonym of complete.

clue.text: Cleaning woman, that is, Tess perhaps portrayed by Robert Bridges's daughter

parts.note: a char or charwoman is a British term for a cleaner

indicators.note: signals that the letters of 'that is' and Tess may be arranged in some other order

parts.note: i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, that is

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady, Tess, has her portrait painted by the poet laureate's daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAR is a British cleaning woman; 'perhaps' rearranges IE (that is) with TESS to give ITESSE. Elizabeth Daryush, Robert Bridges's daughter, published poems titled Charitessi.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grace-like figure is the subject of a collection of poems that the poet laureate's daughter, Elizabeth Daryush, wrote and published.

clue.text: "The flashiest and fustiest that ever corrupted in such an unwill-" (Milton)

definitions.text: "The flashiest and fustiest that ever corrupted in such an unwill-" (Milton)

parts.words: "The flashiest and fustiest that ever corrupted in such an unwill-" (Milton)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Milton, where the broken word continues into the missing noun for a large cask

explanation.surface: A line of Milton's prose is left hanging mid-word.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation runs on to 'unwilling hogshead': Milton, in Areopagitica, likens bad learning to liquor going stale in a cask.
explanation.definitionFit: A large barrel for wine or beer completes Milton's image of stale drink corrupting in its cask.

clue.text: Lodge warning against sharks

parts.note: Thomas Lodge's Elizabethan pamphlet An ... against Usurers, sharks meaning moneylenders

explanation.surface: A beach hut posts a notice about sharks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lodge' looks like a building and 'sharks' like fish; they are the writer Thomas Lodge and loan sharks, the usurers of his 1584 pamphlet.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarum is an old word for a call to arms or warning, the first word of Lodge's pamphlet title.

clue.text: Register phony sort of small child

parts.note: phony means false or fake

indicators.note: says the letters of the child's word are put into a different kind of order

parts.note: a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: Someone records a fake kind of little kid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Register' looks like a verb meaning record; it is a vocal range. 'Small child' is never written out, so the solver must find the word and then rearrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: A falsetto is a singing range above a man's natural voice, and a vocal range is called a register.

clue.text: Get back Giono's book?

definitions.meaning: Jean Giono's 1930 novel, translated as Harvest

explanation.surface: Someone asks to recover a French novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Regain, Jean Giono's novel of Provençal peasant life, shares its French title with the English verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To recover what was lost is a plain synonym, and the French novelist's book bears the identical title.

clue.text: Poet's sort of illustrated pot of Attic shape

definitions.text: Poet's sort of illustrated pot of Attic shape

parts.words: Poet's sort of illustrated pot of Attic shape
parts.note: Keats's ode addresses a decorated urn, calling it 'O Attic shape!'

explanation.surface: A poet admires a painted vase of classical form.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn hails the vase as 'O Attic shape! Fair attitude!'; Attic means Athenian.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats calls his illustrated vase an Attic shape, Attic meaning Athenian, so it is of Greek style.

clue.text: The Bard was his father they say, naturally

definitions.text: The Bard was his father they say, naturally

parts.words: The Bard was his father they say, naturally
parts.note: the Restoration dramatist rumoured to be Shakespeare's illegitimate, or natural, son

explanation.surface: Someone claims, as one would, that Shakespeare was his dad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naturally' looks like 'of course', but a natural son is an illegitimate one; Sir William Davenant let it be thought Shakespeare fathered him.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir William Davenant, poet laureate and playwright, encouraged the rumour that he was Shakespeare's illegitimate son.

clue.text: They put painting first, and second 22 …

definitions.text: They put painting first, and second 22 …

parts.words: They put painting first, and second 22 …
parts.note: people whose priority is painting, and who also take up a stance, as in the next clue

explanation.surface: Some people prioritise painting and then follow on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Painters and sculptors put art first, and they also make their sitters strike a pose, the key part of 22.
explanation.definitionFit: Painters and other creators devote themselves to art, giving painting priority in their lives.

clue.text: … so I strike attitude holding maiden, to take advantage

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
to pose is to strike an attitude

explanation.surface: Someone strikes a pose with a young woman to exploit the situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maiden' looks like a girl, but it is M, the cricket scorer's mark for a maiden over (one with no runs).
explanation.definitionFit: To impose on someone is to exploit their kindness, taking unfair advantage of it.

clue.text: Recalling, they rang a bell for Falstaff in the middle of the night

definitions.text: Recalling, they rang a bell for Falstaff in the middle of the night

parts.words: Recalling, they rang a bell for Falstaff in the middle of the night
parts.note: Falstaff reminisces in Henry IV Part 2

explanation.surface: Bells jogged an old knight's memory late one night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rang a bell' means stirred a memory; Falstaff recalls with Justice Shallow that they 'heard the chimes at midnight'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bells struck at midnight are what Falstaff recalls hearing in his youthful revels with Shallow.

clue.text: Attendant in house that Scott's moneylender occupied

definitions.text: Attendant in house that Scott's moneylender occupied

indicators.note: the servant's name sits inside the words house that, as he lives inside the house

explanation.surface: A servant works in a house rented by a moneylender.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes Seth, a servant in Isaac of York's household in Scott's Ivanhoe; as wordplay, 'in' shows the name tucked inside 'house that'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seth is one of the servants in the household of Isaac of York, the moneylender in Walter Scott's Ivanhoe.

clue.text: One of Goona's was green

parts.note: a character with differently coloured ..., one of them green

explanation.surface: Somebody named Goona had one green feature.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to a character with odd eyes, one green.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes are what come in pairs and in colours, so one of them being green fits the description.

clue.text: Auden seemed to think there was a dog under it

definitions.text: Auden seemed to think there was a dog under it

parts.words: Auden seemed to think there was a dog under it
parts.note: Auden and Isherwood's play The Dog Beneath the ...

explanation.surface: The poet believed a dog was hiding underneath something.
explanation.walkthrough: Auden and Isherwood wrote the verse play 'The Dog Beneath the Skin' (1935).
explanation.definitionFit: The play title puts the dog beneath this body covering, so it is what the dog lies under.

clue.text: His work, to some extent idiotic, sounds as if it later went to the devil

definitions.text: His work, to some extent idiotic, sounds as if it later went to the devil

parts.words: His work, to some extent idiotic, sounds as if it later went to the devil
parts.note: the novelist who wrote The Idiot and, later, The Devils (also called The Possessed)

explanation.surface: A writer's output is partly foolish and heads downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'idiotic' and 'the devil' sound like criticism; they point to The Idiot (1869) and the later novel The Devils (1872).
explanation.definitionFit: Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote The Idiot and then The Devils, so his work moved from idiocy to devilry.

clue.text: High flier, in whom the reader never loses interest…

indicators.note: the bird is found within the words that follow, as if living in them

explanation.surface: A star performer who keeps readers gripped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High flier' looks like a high achiever but is the sea eagle; 'in whom' says it is tucked inside 'the reader never'. The rest of the clue completes the surface and leads into 29.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne, or white-tailed sea eagle, is a large bird that soars high over coasts.

clue.text: … acknowledges novel crises gone

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of crises gone take a new form

explanation.surface: Someone admits that fresh troubles have passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book or an adjective for crises, but it signals rearranging CRISES GONE.
explanation.definitionFit: To recognise something is to acknowledge or accept it officially.
